title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia is bad news for Anthropic. Here's why.
excerpt: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia revives an AI rivalry that threatens Anthropic's business model as AI stocks rally.
content_html:

Most AI stocks surged on Monday following Jensen Huang's dramatic return as Nvidia CEO.

There's one notable exception: Anthropic.

Shares of the recently public AI company fell on Monday, even as Nvidia stock soared and investors celebrate the return of one of the industry's most influential leaders.

What's going on?

The answer lies in a battle over the future of AI, with Huang and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on opposing sides.

Last week, I wrote that Huang's ouster was potentially the best thing to happen to Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster IPO.

Now he's back. And the opposite may be true.

Under Huang, Nvidia was building an alternative AI ecosystem that threatened Anthropic's business model.

Anthropic spends billions of dollars developing powerful AI models that it keeps tightly controlled. Customers generally pay to access this technology.

Huang championed a different approach: Open-weight AI models that companies can download, modify, and run themselves, without paying Anthropic every time they use AI.

Nvidia was investing heavily in this world, developing its own Nemotron models and backing startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines, and Poolside.

The strategy made sense for Nvidia. The more AI models companies run themselves, the more demand there could be for Nvidia's chips. But it threatened Anthropic's ability to charge premium prices for its technology.

One AI startup CEO described the rivalry to me as a "Cold War," with Nvidia on a collision course with the leading AI labs.

There was another important disagreement.

Amodei pushed for strict restrictions on China's access to advanced American AI chips. Huang opposed those limits, arguing they would encourage Chinese competitors.

Huang's removal appeared to strengthen Amodei's position, especially after Washington imposed tougher restrictions on China's access to American AI technology.

Now Huang is back in charge, with the power to resume his push for more open models.

Of course, one day's stock movements don't prove that this is the only thing driving share moves. Anthropic's modest decline could have other explanations. But the contrast is striking.

The AI industry's biggest champion of open models is back. And one of the biggest companies betting on closed models suddenly faces a familiar, formidable opponent, again.
